opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think one thing people overlook is that when the cost of something drops dramatically, demand often grows rather than shrinks. There's a lot of conversation about AI replacing lawyers, and certainly some tasks, like first-pass document review or drafting routine contracts, are getting much cheaper. But the lazy assumption is that the legal market just shrinks.

What I think is more likely, and I could be wrong, is that a lot of people who today simply go without legal help, because it's too expensive or too intimidating, will start getting it. Think of a small business owner who signs a lease without anyone reading it, or a tenant who doesn't know their rights. If you can get decent legal guidance for a few dollars instead of a few hundred an hour, the total amount of legal work being done could go up a lot, even if the price per unit falls.

The second thing people overlook is that the hard part often isn't the model. It's the workflow. A law firm, a corporate legal team, a court system: these all have very specific processes, liability concerns, and ways of checking work. The teams that win won't just be the ones with the best large language model. They'll be the ones who deeply understand how a legal task actually gets done, break it into steps, and build agentic workflows where AI does some steps, a human reviews others, and the whole system is reliable enough that people trust it.

And I'd add one more: the role of the lawyer shifts. Junior lawyers traditionally learned by doing a lot of grunt work. If AI does that work, we need to rethink how people build judgment. I don't think that's a reason to slow down, but it's a real design problem for the profession. My general advice, for lawyers and frankly for everyone, is to learn to use these tools now. People who use AI well are going to be much more productive than those who don't, and that gap is going to matter a lot more than whether AI replaces any particular job outright.

r001.rationale: The response discusses lower legal-service costs and potentially greater demand, but does not say AI is drawing high-value capital into markets that normally would not attract it.

r002.rationale: The response discusses legal workflows and lawyers adapting to AI, but does not say AI is attracting strong engineers who previously avoided the legal sector.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing people most overlook is that "legal" isn't one market, it's a bundle of hundreds of very specific tasks, and AI's effect on each of them is wildly different.

When people talk about AI and law, they tend to think at the level of the job: will AI replace lawyers, yes or no? That framing almost always leads you astray. The way I find it useful to think about it is to break the work down into tasks. A lawyer might spend time on contract review, legal research, drafting, client counseling, negotiation, court appearances, business development. Some of those, like first-pass document review or pulling relevant precedents, are very amenable to automation today. Others, like reading the room in a negotiation or giving a client judgment about whether to settle, are much harder, and I don't think we're close on those. So the honest answer is that AI will automate parts of many jobs rather than whole jobs, and the economics follow from which parts.

The second thing people miss is where the value actually accrues. There's a lot of attention on the big firms, but a huge amount of legal work in the world simply doesn't get done today because it's too expensive. Small businesses that never get a contract reviewed, individuals who never get advice on a lease or a dispute. When the cost of a task falls by an order of magnitude, you don't just redistribute the existing pie, you create demand that wasn't being served at all. I think that expansion of the market is underappreciated relative to the displacement story.

And the third thing is that the hard part turns out not to be the model. It's the workflow and the data around it. Law firms have very specific document formats, very specific risk tolerances, confidentiality requirements, a need for traceability back to a source. Getting a demo to work is easy. Getting something a partner will actually trust in front of a client, where a mistake has real consequences, takes a lot of unglamorous engineering. That last mile is where most of the real work is, and it's also where I think a lot of the durable companies will get built.

r001.rationale: The response says lower task costs can create new demand for underserved legal services, but it does not state that AI is drawing high-value capital into markets that would not normally attract it.

r002.rationale: The response discusses workflow engineering and durable companies, but does not say that AI is attracting strong engineers who previously avoided the legal sector.

astra-6.text:
I think people sometimes assume that there’s a fixed amount of legal work to be done, so if AI makes lawyers more efficient, we’ll need fewer lawyers. But there’s a lot of unmet demand for legal services. Many people and small businesses don’t get legal advice because it’s too expensive.

If AI brings that cost down, more people may be able to afford help reviewing a contract or resolving a dispute. So the question isn’t just how much existing work we can automate. It’s also how much additional demand becomes viable at a lower price. Some tasks will shrink, but the overall market could expand. How those two effects balance out is something we need to examine, rather than assuming productivity gains translate directly into job losses.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unmet demand and possible market expansion, but does not state that AI is drawing high-value capital into otherwise unattractive markets.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention strong engineers or say AI makes legal work attractive to engineers who previously avoided the sector.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people sometimes focus too much on which jobs AI can automate, and not enough on how demand changes when a service becomes much cheaper. Take legal services. There are a lot of people and small businesses that would benefit from legal advice but simply can’t afford it today. They sign contracts they don’t fully understand, or they don’t pursue a legitimate claim because the cost is too high.

If AI brings down the cost of providing those services, the market could expand substantially. That doesn’t mean every lawyer benefits or that there won’t be disruption. But automating part of a lawyer’s work doesn’t automatically imply a proportional reduction in the number of lawyers. You also have to ask: How much unmet demand is there, and what new services become possible at that lower price?

r001.rationale: The response discusses lower service costs and possible market growth, but does not say AI is drawing high-value capital into markets that would not normally attract it.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention strong engineers or say AI makes the legal sector attractive to engineers who previously avoided it.
